Together, the three companies --- the \"Big Three\" --- control approximately 48% of the relevant market (22% + 15% + 11% = 48%). Their coordinated refusal to deal excluded Prairie Harvest from access to nearly half of all available wholesale supply in the market.

148\. The concerted refusal to deal was not the product of independent business decisions by three unrelated companies arriving at the same conclusion by coincidence. It was the product of a deliberate and coordinated agreement among the Big Three to exclude Prairie Harvest from the market, punish it for its resistance to Greenfield\'s pricing dictates, and deter other retailers from engaging in intrabrand price competition.

149\. The agreement among the Big Three was reached at or around the time of the Midwest Organic Trade Association (\"MOTA\") Annual Conference, held April 12--14, 2024, in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and was implemented through the coordinated refusal to supply Prairie Harvest during the May through August 2024 period.

150\. The evidence of this conspiracy includes the following. First, the parallel refusal to deal by all three of the Big Three distributors during the same time period --- May through August 2024 --- is itself strong circumstantial evidence of concerted action. The simultaneous nature of the refusals, combined with the absence of any independent business justification, renders the inference of conspiracy more plausible than the inference of unilateral action.

151\. Second, the MOTA Annual Conference in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, held April 12--14, 2024, provided the opportunity and setting for executives from Greenfield, Heartland, and Great Lakes to discuss Prairie Harvest\'s termination and to reach an agreement regarding the coordinated refusal to deal. On information and belief, senior executives from all three companies attended the conference and participated in discussions regarding Prairie Harvest. The conference took place during the critical window between Greenfield\'s termination notice (March 15, 2024) and the effective date of the termination (April 30, 2024) --- precisely the period during which coordination regarding post-termination supply would have been most valuable to the conspirators.

152\. Third, the June 3, 2024 internal Heartland email from Kevin Marsh (Exhibit C) demonstrates that Heartland had specific knowledge of Greenfield\'s termination of Prairie Harvest and used that knowledge as the basis for its own refusal to onboard Prairie Harvest. The email\'s reference to Greenfield having \"dropped\" Prairie Harvest reflects insider knowledge of the termination. The email\'s invocation of \"standard credit review\" procedures as a basis for subjecting Prairie Harvest to \"enhanced due diligence\" was pretextual --- Prairie Harvest was a well-established retailer with \$38.2 million in annual revenue and a decade of successful operations, and its credit profile did not warrant the enhanced scrutiny that Heartland imposed.

153\. Fourth, the motivation for the conspiracy is readily apparent. Greenfield had a direct interest in ensuring that Prairie Harvest could not find alternative supply after termination, because the ability of terminated dealers to secure alternative supply would undermine the coercive power of Greenfield\'s exclusive dealing and resale price maintenance schemes. If retailers knew that they could simply switch to a competing distributor after being terminated by Greenfield, Greenfield\'s threats of termination would lose their deterrent effect. By coordinating with Heartland and Great Lakes to refuse supply to Prairie Harvest, Greenfield ensured that the termination would be maximally punitive and that other dealers would observe that resistance to Greenfield\'s demands led to total market exclusion.

154\. The Big Three collectively control 48% of the relevant market. Their coordinated refusal to deal effectively excluded Prairie Harvest from nearly half of all available wholesale supply in the six-state Midwest region. The smaller distributors in the market, which collectively account for the remaining 52% of market volume, could not provide a viable substitute for the Big Three. Many of these smaller distributors serve limited geographic areas, carry narrow product assortments, and lack the refrigerated logistics infrastructure necessary to supply Prairie Harvest\'s twelve-store operation across central and southern Illinois.

155\. The combined market power of the conspirators meant that their coordinated refusal to deal had a devastating effect on Prairie Harvest. Prairie Harvest was unable to maintain its full product assortment, experienced severe inventory shortages, lost customer traffic and sales, and suffered damage to its business reputation. Several of Prairie Harvest\'s stores operated at substantially reduced capacity during the May through August 2024 period, and Prairie Harvest faced the prospect of permanent store closures.

156\. The group boycott also harmed competition more broadly. By punishing Prairie Harvest for engaging in price competition, the Big Three sent a chilling message to all retailers in the six-state Midwest region: any dealer that challenges the pricing dictates of the major distributors risks being cut off from all supply sources. This deterrent effect reduces the incentives for retailers to compete on price, contributing to higher consumer prices for organic and natural food products throughout the region.

157\. A group boycott among horizontal competitors is per se unlawful under Section 1 of the Sherman Act. The Supreme Court has recognized that concerted refusals to deal by competitors are among the most pernicious forms of anticompetitive conduct, warranting per se condemnation without the need for elaborate analysis of competitive effects. The Big Three\'s coordinated refusal to supply Prairie Harvest fits squarely within the per se category of group boycotts.

158\. Alternatively, even if the rule of reason applies, the coordinated refusal to deal is unreasonable given: (a) the combined market power of the conspirators (48% of the relevant market); (b) the severe injury inflicted on Prairie Harvest; (c) the broader chilling effect on intrabrand price competition; (d) the absence of any procompetitive justification for the coordinated refusal; and (e) the availability of less restrictive alternatives that would not have required the complete exclusion of Prairie Harvest from the market.

159\. As a direct and proximate result of the group boycott, Prairie Harvest has suffered antitrust injury. Prairie Harvest has been injured in its business and property in an amount to be proven at trial.

160\. Under Section 4 of the Clayton Act, 15 U.S.C. § 15, Prairie Harvest is entitled to recover threefold the damages it has sustained, plus the cost of suit, including a reasonable attorney\'s fee.

**Count IV: Violation of Section 2 of the Sherman Act --- Monopolization and Attempted Monopolization**

161\. Plaintiff Prairie Harvest Natural Foods LLC re-alleges and incorporates by reference the allegations contained in all preceding paragraphs of this Complaint as though fully set forth herein.

162\. This claim is brought pursuant to Section 2 of the Sherman Act, 15 U.S.C. § 2, which prohibits monopolization and attempted monopolization of any part of trade or commerce among the several States.

**Monopolization**

163\. Greenfield possesses monopoly power in the relevant market for organic and natural food wholesale distribution services in the six-state Midwest region. Monopoly power is the power to control prices or exclude competition. Greenfield\'s monopoly power is evidenced by the following factors.

164\. First, Greenfield controls approximately 22% of the relevant market and is the single largest distributor in the six-state Midwest region. Greenfield\'s market share exceeds that of the next-largest competitor, Heartland Provisions Co., by 7 percentage points and exceeds that of the third-largest competitor, Great Lakes Natural Supply, by 11 percentage points. Greenfield\'s market share has grown steadily from 14% in 2017 to 22% in 2023 --- an increase of 8 percentage points over six years --- reflecting its progressive accumulation of market power.

165\. Second, the relevant market is highly concentrated. The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index for the relevant market, when the coordinated behavior of the Big Three is taken into account, is 3,730 --- far above the 2,500 thr

eshold for a \"highly concentrated\" market. This level of concentration creates structural conditions in which a dominant firm such as Greenfield can exercise monopoly power by leveraging its position to exclude competitors and coerce dealers.

166\. Third, significant barriers to entry prevent new competitors from entering the market and challenging Greenfield\'s dominance. These barriers include the substantial capital investment required to establish regional distribution center networks, refrigerated transport fleets, and cold-chain logistics infrastructure; the difficulty of establishing supply relationships with organic producers and manufacturers; the time required to build a retail account base of sufficient density to achieve efficient route economics; and the lock-up effect of Greenfield\'s exclusive dealing arrangements, which prevent potential competitors from accessing approximately 15.4% of the market.

167\. Greenfield has willfully acquired and maintained its monopoly power through anticompetitive conduct rather than through legitimate competition on the merits. Specifically, Greenfield has: (a) implemented exclusive dealing arrangements (the ADAs) that foreclose approximately 15.4% of the relevant market to competing distributors; (b) imposed resale price maintenance policies that suppress intrabrand price competition and prevent dealers from offering competitive prices to consumers; and (c) coordinated with Heartland and Great Lakes to implement a group boycott that excluded Prairie Harvest from the market and deterred other dealers from engaging in competitive conduct.

168\. These exclusionary practices are not the conduct of a firm competing on the merits of its products, prices, and services. They are the conduct of a firm that has obtained a dominant market position and is abusing that position to foreclose competition, punish resistant dealers, and entrench its monopoly. Greenfield\'s anticompetitive conduct has enabled it to raise and maintain prices above competitive levels, to restrict output and product availability, and to diminish the quality and diversity of distribution services available to retailers in the six-state Midwest region.

169\. Greenfield\'s willful acquisition and maintenance of monopoly power in the relevant market through the anticompetitive conduct described herein constitutes monopolization in violation of Section 2 of the Sherman Act, 15 U.S.C. § 2.

170\. As a direct and proximate result of Greenfield\'s monopolization, Prairie Harvest has suffered antitrust injury and damages.

**Attempted Monopolization**

171\. In the alternative, Greenfield has engaged in attempted monopolization of the relevant market in violation of Section 2 of the Sherman Act. Attempted monopolization requires: (1) that the defendant engaged in predatory or anticompetitive conduct; (2) with a specific intent to monopolize; and (3) that there is a dangerous probability that the defendant will succeed in monopolizing the relevant market.

172\. Greenfield has engaged in predatory and anticompetitive conduct, as described in detail throughout this Complaint, including exclusive dealing arrangements, resale price maintenance, and a coordinated group boycott. This conduct is exclusionary and is directed at foreclosing competition, punishing competitive behavior by dealers, and expanding Greenfield\'s market share at the expense of competitors and consumers.

173\. Greenfield has acted with the specific intent to monopolize the relevant market. This intent is evidenced by: (a) Greenfield\'s escalating market share, which has grown from 14% to 22% over six years, reflecting a deliberate strategy of market share accumulation; (b) Greenfield\'s imposition of increasingly restrictive exclusive dealing requirements that are designed to foreclose competitors from accessing retail accounts; (c) Greenfield\'s enforcement of minimum resale prices to suppress intrabrand competition and maintain artificially high margins; and (d) Greenfield\'s coordination with Heartland and Great Lakes to exclude dealers who resist its pricing dictates, demonstrating an intent to use its market power to punish and deter competitive conduct.

174\. There is a dangerous probability that Greenfield will succeed in monopolizing the relevant market. Greenfield\'s market share has grown from 14% to 22% over six years, and at its current growth trajectory, Greenfield\'s market share will approach 30% within the next five years. The exclusive dealing arrangements lock in Greenfield\'s existing dealer base and prevent competitors from winning business through competitive efforts. The coordinated group boycott with Heartland and Great Lakes further suppresses competitive entry and expansion.

175\. The barriers to entry described above --- including the capital requirements for distribution infrastructure, the difficulty of establishing supply and customer relationships, and the lock-up effect of the exclusive dealing arrangements --- ensure that new competitors cannot enter the market in sufficient scale to offset Greenfield\'s continued growth. Absent intervention by this Court, Greenfield will continue its trajectory toward full monopolization of the organic and natural food wholesale distribution market in the six-state Midwest region.

176\. The relevant market is already highly concentrated, with an HHI of 3,730, and Greenfield\'s continued growth will only increase this concentration further. The smaller distributors in the market --- the approximately 40 firms that collectively hold 36% of the market --- lack the scale, infrastructure, and resources to resist Greenfield\'s exclusionary practices. Many of these smaller distributors are vulnerable to the same tactics that Greenfield deployed against Prairie Harvest: exclusive dealing arrangements that capture their accounts, pricing restrictions that suppress their competitive options, and coordinated boycotts that deny them supply.

177\. As a direct and proximate result of Greenfield\'s attempted monopolization, Prairie Harvest has suffered antitrust injury and damages.

178\. Under Section 4 of the Clayton Act, 15 U.S.C. § 15, Prairie Harvest is entitled to recover threefold the damages it has sustained, plus the cost of suit, including a reasonable attorney\'s fee.

**Count V: Violation of Section 3 of the Clayton Act --- Exclusive Dealing**

179\. Plaintiff Prairie Harvest Natural Foods LLC re-alleges and incorporates by reference the allegations contained in all preceding paragraphs of this Complaint as though fully set forth herein.

180\. This claim is brought pursuant to Section 3 of the Clayton Act, 15 U.S.C. § 14.

181\. Section 3 of the Clayton Act provides that it shall be unlawful for any person engaged in commerce to lease or make a sale or contract for sale of goods, wares, merchandise, machinery, supplies, or other commodities, on the condition, agreement, or understanding that the lessee or purchaser thereof shall not use or deal in the goods, wares, merchandise, machinery, supplies, or other commodities of a competitor or competitors of the lessor or seller, where the effect of such condition, agreement, or understanding may be to substantially lessen competition or tend to create a monopoly in any line of commerce.

182\. Greenfield is a person engaged in commerce within the meaning of Section 3 of the Clayton Act. Greenfield sells organic and natural food products --- which are goods, wares, and merchandise within the meaning of Section 3 --- to retailers across the six-state Midwest region.

183\. Greenfield\'s Authorized Dealer Agreements, including the 70% minimum purchase requirement set forth in Section 7.2, constitute sales or contracts for sale of goods on the condition that the purchaser shall not deal in the goods of Greenfield\'s competitors. The 70% minimum purchase requirement effectively precludes dealers from purchasing more than 30% of their organic and natural food products from distributors other than Greenfield, thereby substantially restricting dealers\' ability to deal in the goods supplied by Greenfield\'s competitors.

184\. Approximately 1,900 of Greenfield\'s 2,800 retail accounts have executed ADAs containing the 70% minimum purchase requirement. The scope and penetration of the ADA program are substantial and reflect Greenfield\'s systematic effort to lock up a large share of the retail accounts in the relevant market through exclusive dealing arrangements.

185\. The effect of Greenfield\'s exclusive dealing arrangements is to substantially lessen competition in the relevant market for organic and natural food wholesale distribution services in the six-state Midwest region. Approximately 15.4% of the relevant market is foreclosed to competing distributors as a result of the ADA exclusivity provisions. This substantial foreclosure impairs the ability of competing distributors to compete for retail accounts, achieve efficient scale, and maintain viable distribution networks.

186\. The foreclosure caused by Greenfield\'s exclusive dealing arrangements reduces the number of distribution alternatives available to retailers, diminishes competitive discipline on pricing and service quality, and insulates Greenfield from the competitive pressures that would otherwise constrain its market behavior. Retailers that are bound by ADAs cannot easily switch to competing distributors, even when those competitors offer better prices, broader product selection, or superior service.

187\. The exclusive dealing arrangements also increase barriers to entry in the relevant market. New and smaller distributors seeking to enter or expand in the six-state Midwest region must compete for accounts that are already locked into exclusive relationships with Greenfield. The lock-up effect of the three-year ADA terms and automatic renewal provisions means that a large portion of the addressable market is unavailable to potential competitors at any given time, significantly increasing the difficulty and cost of market entry.

188\. The cumulative effect of these competitive harms is to suppress competition, raise distribution costs, reduce service innovation, and ultimately harm consumers by limiting their access to competitively priced organic and natural food products.

189\. The exclusive dealing arrangements also tend to create a monopoly within the meaning of Section 3 of the Clayton Act. Greenfield\'s market share has grown from 14% in 2017 to 22% in 2023 --- a period that coincides with the introduction and expansion of the ADA program. The ADA program has been the primary engine of Greenfield\'s market share growth, enabling Greenfield to lock in existing accounts, prevent competitor defection, and progressively accumulate a larger share of the relevant market.

190\. If the ADA program is permitted to continue, Greenfield\'s market share will continue to grow, further concentrating the market and increasing Greenfield\'s ability to exercise unilateral control over pricing, supply, and distribution terms. The tendency of Greenfield\'s exclusive dealing arrangements to create a monopoly is not speculative --- it is demonstrated by the trajectory of Greenfield\'s market share growth over the past six years.

191\. As a direct and proximate result of Greenfield\'s exclusive dealing arrangements in violation of Section 3 of the Clayton Act, Prairie Harvest has suffered injury and damages. Prairie Harvest was bound by the exclusivity provisions of its own ADA, which prevented it from developing robust alternative supply relationships. When Greenfield terminated Prairie Harvest, the exclusive dealing arrangements had already foreclosed the market to the extent that Prairie Harvest was unable to secure adequate alternative supply.

192\. Prairie Harvest seeks damages, treble damages as provided by Section 4 of the Clayton Act (15 U.S.C. § 15), costs of suit, and a reasonable attorney\'s fee.

195\. Section 3 of the Illinois Antitrust Act, 740 ILCS 10/3, provides that every contract, combination, or conspiracy in restraint of trade or commerce in the State of Illinois is illegal. The Illinois Antitrust Act is to be construed in harmony with federal antitrust law, including the Sherman Act and the Clayton Act, as applicable.

196\. Greenfield\'s exclusive dealing arrangements, as implemented through the ADA program and the 70% minimum purchase requirement, constitute contracts in restraint of trade or commerce in the State of Illinois in violation of 740 ILCS 10/3. These arrangements unreasonably restrain competition in the organic and natural food wholesale distribution market by foreclosing competing distributors from a substantial share of the market and by locking retailers into exclusive supply relationships with Greenfield.

197\. Greenfield\'s resale price maintenance policies, as implemented through Sections 9.1 and 9.3 of the ADA and enforced through Greenfield\'s field representative monitoring program and escalating warnings and terminations, constitute contracts, combinations, or conspiracies in restraint of trade or commerce in the State of Illinois in violation of 740 ILCS 10/3. These policies fix the minimum resale prices of Greenfield-branded products, suppress intrabrand price competition, and result in artificially inflated consumer prices for organic and natural food products sold in Illinois.

198\. Greenfield\'s coordinated group boycott with Heartland Provisions Co. and Great Lakes Natural Supply, Inc., as described herein, constitutes a combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade or commerce in the State of Illinois in violation of 740 ILCS 10/3. The coordinated refusal to deal with Prairie Harvest excluded Prairie Harvest from access to a substantial portion of the wholesale distribution market and caused severe harm to Prairie Harvest\'s business and to competition in the Illinois market.

199\. The anticompetitive conduct described herein occurred in and directly affected trade and commerce within the State of Illinois. Prairie Harvest operates twelve retail stores in central and southern Illinois, each of which purchases organic and natural food products from wholesale distributors for resale to Illinois consumers. Greenfield is headquartered in Evanston, Illinois, and conducts substantial business throughout the State of Illinois. The anticompetitive conduct at issue --- including the execution and enforcement of ADAs, the enforcement of resale price restrictions, and the termination of Prairie Harvest --- occurred in significant part within the State of Illinois.

200\. The harm to competition and to consumers resulting from Greenfield\'s conduct is concentrated in the State of Illinois, where Prairie Harvest operates and where a significant portion of Greenfield\'s dealer base is located. Illinois consumers have been harmed by higher prices for organic and natural food products, reduced retail competition, and diminished product availability resulting from Greenfield\'s anticompetitive scheme.

201\. Under Section 7(2) of the Illinois Antitrust Act, 740 ILCS 10/7(2), any person who has been injured in its business or property by reason of a violation of the Illinois Antitrust Act may bring an action for damages and injunctive relief. Prairie Harvest is a \"person\" within the meaning of the Illinois Antitrust Act and has been injured in its business and property by reason of Greenfield\'s violations of 740 ILCS 10/3, as described herein.

202\. Prairie Harvest has suffered substantial damages as a result of Greenfield\'s violations of the Illinois Antitrust Act, including lost profits, lost customer relationships, diminished product availability, and damage to business reputation and goodwill, in amounts to be proven at trial.

203\. Prairie Harvest seeks compensatory damages, treble damages as provided by the Illinois Antitrust Act, costs of suit, and reasonable attorneys\' fees, pursuant to 740 ILCS 10/5.

204\. Plaintiff Prairie Harvest Natural Foods LLC re-alleges and incorporates by reference the allegations contained in all preceding paragraphs of this Complaint as though fully set forth herein.

205\. This claim is brought under the common law of the State of Illinois for tortious interference with business relations, also known as tortious interference with prospective economic advantage.

206\. Prairie Harvest had valid and existing business relationships with its retail customers across central and southern Illinois, who regularly patronized Prairie Harvest\'s twelve stores for the purchase of organic and natural food products. These customer relationships were the foundation of Prairie Harvest\'s business and were developed over a period of ten years through consistent product quality, competitive pricing, community engagement, and reliable service.

207\. Prairie Harvest also had valid and existing business relationships and reasonable expectancies of continued and future business relationships with its suppliers, business partners, and commercial counterparts, including relationships with producers, manufacturers, and other distributors in the organic and natural food industry.

208\. Greenfield was aware of Prairie Harvest\'s customer relationships, supplier relationships, and reasonable expectancies of continued business. 209\. Greenfield intentionally and unjustifiably interfered with Prairie Harvest\'s business relationships by: (a) terminating Prairie Harvest\'s Authorized Dealer Agreement on pretextual grounds, thereby cutting off Prairie Harvest\'s primary source of product supply and preventing Prairie Harvest from adequately serving its customers; (b) coordinating with Heartland Provisions Co. and Great Lakes Natural Supply, Inc. to refuse to supply Prairie Harvest, thereby preventing Prairie Harvest from obtaining alternative supply and compounding the disruption to Prairie Harvest\'s business operations; and (c) imposing and enforcing exclusive dealing arrangements (the 70% minimum purchase requirement) that prevented Prairie Harvest from establishing and maintaining supply relationships with competing distributors during the term of the ADA, leaving Prairie Harvest without a fallback supply network when Greenfield terminated the relationship.

210\. Greenfield\'s interference was accomplished through improper means, including the use of unlawful exclusive dealing arrangements, unlawful resale price maintenance, and an unlawful coordinated group boycott --- all of which constitute violations of federal and state antitrust laws as alleged in Counts I through VI of this Complaint. 211\. Greenfield\'s interference was also motivated by an improper purpose --- to punish Prairie Harvest for offering competitive retail prices to consumers and for purchasing products from competing distributors, and to deter other dealers throughout the six-state Midwest region from engaging in similar competitive conduct. 212\. Greenfield\'s conduct was willful, wanton, and malicious. Greenfield knew that the termination of Prairie Harvest\'s supply relationship, combined with the coordinated group boycott, would cause severe and potentially irreparable harm to Prairie Harvest\'s business. 213\. Greenfield\'s tortious interference was the proximate cause of significant harm to Prairie Harvest\'s business relationships and economic expectancies. 214\. As a direct and proximate result of Greenfield\'s tortious interference with business relations, Prairie Harvest has suffered damages, including lost profits, lost customer relationships, reputational harm, and other consequential damages, in an amount to be proven at trial. 215\. Prairie Harvest is entitled to compensatory damages sufficient to make it whole for the harm caused by Greenfield\'s tortious conduct, including lost profits, lost business value, and such other damages as may be proven at trial.

The Parties shall negotiate in good faith for a period of thirty (30) days following delivery of such notice before either Party may commence any formal legal proceeding.
290	
291	**Section 14.3 --- Jurisdiction and Venue**
292	
293	Any action, suit, or proceeding arising out of or relating to this Agreement that is not resolved through negotiation under Section 14.2 shall be brought exclusively in the federal or state courts located in Cook County, Illinois, and each Party irrevocably submits to the exclusive personal jurisdiction of such courts and waives any objection to venue in such courts, including any objection based on forum non conveniens.
294	
295	**Section 14.4 --- Attorneys\' Fees**
296	
297	In any action, suit, or proceeding to enforce this Agreement or to resolve any dispute arising hereunder, the prevailing Party shall be entitled to recover its reasonable attorneys\' fees, expert witness fees, court costs, and other litigation expenses from the non-prevailing Party, in addition to any other relief to which the prevailing Party may be entitled.
298	
299	**[ARTICLE 15 --- GENERAL PROVISIONS]{.underline}**
300	
301	**Section 15.1 --- Entire Agreement**
302	
303	This Agreement, including all Exhibits attached hereto and incorporated herein by reference, constitutes the entire agreement between the Parties with respect to the subject matter hereof and supersedes all prior and contemporaneous agreements, understandings, negotiations, representations, and warranties, whether written or oral, relating to the subject matter of this Agreement. This Agreement supersedes and replaces any prior supply arrangement, purchase agreement, or informal business relationship between Company and Dealer with respect to the purchase and resale of Authorized Products.
304	
305	**Section 15.2 --- Amendments**
306	
307	This Agreement may be amended, modified, or supplemented only by a written instrument duly executed by authorized representatives of both Parties. No oral modification or waiver shall be effective.
308	
309	**Section 15.3 --- Assignment**
310	
311	Neither Party may assign, transfer, or delegate this Agreement or any of its rights or obligations hereunder without the other Party\'s prior written consent, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Notwithstanding the foregoing, Company may assign this Agreement without Dealer\'s consent to an affiliate, a successor entity, or in connection with a merger, acquisition, reorganization, or sale of substantially all of Company\'s assets, provided that the assignee assumes all of Company\'s obligations under this Agreement.
312	
313	**Section 15.4 --- Notices**
314	
315	All notices, requests, demands, consents, and other communications required or permitted under this Agreement shall be in writing and shall be deemed duly delivered when: (a) delivered personally; (b) sent by certified mail, return receipt requested, postage prepaid; or (c) sent by nationally recognized overnight courier service with tracking capability, to the addresses set forth below (or to such other address as may be designated by a Party in writing in accordance with this Section):
316	
317	> If to Company: Greenfield Organics, Inc.
318	>
319	> Attn: Senior Vice President of Sales & Distribution
320	>
321	> 2750 Central Park Avenue Evanston, Illinois 60201
322	>
323	> If to Dealer: Prairie Harvest Natural Foods LLC
324	>
325	> Attn: Chief Executive Officer
326	>
327	> 415 South Neil Street, Suite 200 Champaign, Illinois 61820
328	
329	Notices sent by certified mail shall be deemed delivered three (3) business days after deposit in the United States mail. Notices sent by overnight courier shall be deemed delivered one (1) business day after deposit with the courier service.
330	
331	**Section 15.5 --- Severability**
332	
333	If any provision of this Agreement is held by a court of competent jurisdiction to be invalid, illegal, or unenforceable under applicable law, such provision shall be modified to the minimum extent necessary to make it valid and enforceable, and the remaining provisions of this Agreement shall continue in full force and effect.
334	
335	**Section 15.6 --- Waiver**
336	
337	The failure of either Party to enforce any provision of this Agreement at any time shall not constitute a waiver of such Party\'s right to enforce such provision or any other provision of this Agreement in the future. No waiver shall be effective unless made in writing and signed by the waiving Party.
338	
339	**Section 15.7 --- Force Majeure**
340	
341	Neither Party shall be liable for any delay or failure in performance of its obligations under this Agreement (other than payment obligations) to the extent caused by events beyond its reasonable control, including without limitation natural disasters, epidemics, pandemics, acts of God, government actions or restrictions, embargoes, sanctions, labor disputes, strikes, fire, flood, war, terrorism, civil unrest, or supply chain disruptions. The affected Party shall provide prompt notice of the force majeure event and shall use commercially reasonable efforts to mitigate its impact.
342	
343	**Section 15.8 --- Counterparts**
344	
345	This Agreement may be executed in any number of counterparts, each of which shall be deemed an original and all of which together shall constitute one and the same instrument. Execution and delivery of this Agreement by facsimile or electronic transmission (including PDF) shall be deemed to be original execution and delivery for all purposes.
346	
347	**Section 15.9 --- Relationship to Other Agreements**
348	
349	This Agreement is Greenfield Organics, Inc.\'s standard Authorized Dealer Agreement form, adopted effective January 1, 2020, and utilized by Company in connection with its authorized dealer program across its dealer network. To the extent any prior informal supply arrangement, course of dealing, or purchase agreement between Company and Dealer is inconsistent with the terms set forth herein, the terms of this Agreement shall control and govern the relationship between the Parties from and after the Effective Date.

376	
377	**DEALER TERRITORY**
378	
379	The \"Dealer Territory\" for purposes of this Agreement shall consist of central and southern Illinois, defined as all counties within the State of Illinois located south of Interstate 80 and east of Interstate 55, including but not limited to the following counties: Champaign County, Vermilion County, Macon County, Sangamon County, Coles County, Douglas County, Edgar County, Piatt County, DeWitt County, Moultrie County, Shelby County, Christian County, Montgomery County, Effingham County, Clark County, Cumberland County, and surrounding counties in which Dealer operates one or more retail locations as of the Effective Date.

381	The Dealer Territory designation is non-exclusive. Company expressly retains the unrestricted right to appoint additional authorized dealers within the Dealer Territory, to sell Authorized Products directly to retail customers or institutional accounts within the Dealer Territory, and to distribute Authorized Products through any other distribution channels operating within or serving the Dealer Territory. This Exhibit A does not confer upon Dealer any exclusive rights, protected territory, or right of first refusal with respect to the distribution of Authorized Products within the Dealer Territory.
382	
383	**[EXHIBIT B]{.underline}**
384	
385	**VOLUME DISCOUNT SCHEDULE**
386	
387	The following volume-based pricing discounts shall apply to Dealer\'s purchases of Authorized Products during the Term, subject to the terms and conditions set forth in Section 4.3 of the Agreement:
388

390	  **Tier**                **Annual Purchase Volume (Wholesale Invoice Value)**   **Discount Off Base Wholesale Price**
391	  ----------------------- ------------------------------------------------------ ---------------------------------------
392	  Tier 1                  \$500,000 --- \$999,999                                0% (Base wholesale price)

395

397

399

402	
403	**Calculation Methodology:** Volume discount tiers shall be determined based on Dealer\'s aggregate dollar volume of purchases of Authorized Products (measured by wholesale invoice value) during the trailing twelve (12)-month period. Applicable discounts shall be applied as credits against subsequent invoices and shall be recalculated on a quarterly basis. For the initial twelve (12)-month period of the Term, the discount tier shall be determined based on Dealer\'s annualized purchase volume calculated from actual purchases during the period elapsed since the Effective Date.
404	
405	**Tier Adjustments:** If Dealer\'s trailing twelve-month purchase volume causes Dealer to move to a higher or lower discount tier, the new discount rate shall become effective as of the first day of the calendar quarter following the quarter in which the tier change is confirmed. Company shall notify Dealer of any tier adjustment via the Dealer Portal.
406	
407	**[EXHIBIT C]{.underline}**
408	
409	**MAP POLICY SUPPLEMENT**

411	This MAP Policy Supplement is incorporated into and forms a part of the Authorized Dealer Agreement between Greenfield Organics, Inc. and Prairie Harvest Natural Foods LLC dated February 1, 2021.

413	**1. MAP Schedule Publication.** Minimum Advertised Prices for all Greenfield-Branded Products are published on the Dealer Portal and are updated quarterly, or more frequently at Company\'s discretion as market conditions warrant. The current MAP schedule is available at dealers.greenfieldorganics.com/map-schedule. Company shall provide Dealer with at least fourteen (14) days\' advance notice of any MAP changes, as set forth in Section 9.1 of the Agreement.

MAP Monitoring.** Company monitors dealer advertising through periodic market surveys, online price monitoring (including automated web crawling of dealer websites and third-party marketplace platforms), field representative reports, and consumer reports. Company\'s monitoring activities are conducted to support the integrity of the Greenfield brand and are not intended to restrict Dealer\'s independent pricing discretion at the point of sale.
422	
423	**4. MAP Violation Procedure.** The following graduated enforcement procedure shall apply to violations of the MAP policy:
424	
425	> • *First Violation:* Written warning issued by Company via the Dealer Portal or direct written communication, identifying the specific product(s) and advertising medium involved.
426	>
427	> • *Second Violation within 12 Months:* Formal notice of non-compliance, documenting the repeat violation and advising Dealer that further violations may result in termination of the Agreement.
428	>
429	> • *Third Violation within 12 Months:* Eligible for termination for cause under Section 12.4(d) of the Agreement, subject to the notice and process requirements set forth therein.
430	
431	**5. Clarification Regarding Scope.** The MAP applies solely to the advertised or publicly displayed price. This MAP Policy does not establish a minimum resale price, and Dealers retain discretion over the actual transaction price charged to consumers at the point of sale.
432

**GREENFIELD ORGANICS, INC.** 2750 Central Park Avenue Evanston, Illinois 60201 Tel: (847) 555-0100 \| Fax: (847) 555-0101 www.greenfieldorganics.com

March 15, 2024

**VIA CERTIFIED MAIL (Return Receipt Requested) AND EMAIL**

Mr. Eli Brogan Founder & Chief Executive Officer Prairie Harvest Natural Foods LLC 415 South Neil Street, Suite 200 Champaign, IL 61820

**Re: Notice of Termination of Authorized Dealer Agreement dated February 1, 2021 (as auto-renewed February 1, 2024)**

Dear Mr. Brogan:

This letter constitutes formal written notice of termination of the Authorized Dealer Agreement (the \"ADA\" or \"Agreement\") by and between Greenfield Organics, Inc. (\"Greenfield\") and Prairie Harvest Natural Foods LLC (\"Prairie Harvest\"), originally executed on February 1, 2021, for an initial three-year term expiring January 31, 2024, and automatically renewed on February 1, 2024, for an additional one-year period pursuant to Section 12.2 of the Agreement. Greenfield hereby terminates the Agreement for cause, effective **April 30, 2024**, pursuant to Section 12.4 of the Agreement, based on repeated material breaches by Prairie Harvest as described below. This letter provides forty-six (46) days\' prior written notice of termination, which exceeds the thirty (30)-day minimum notice period required under Section 12.4 for termination for cause. The grounds for termination are set forth in detail in the sections that follow.

**Violation of Section 7.2 --- Purchase Volume Requirements**

Section 7.2 of the ADA requires that \"at least 70% of Dealer\'s purchases of Organic and Natural Food Products (by dollar volume) shall be sourced from Greenfield\" during the term of the Agreement. Greenfield\'s internal records and third-party purchase data indicate that Prairie Harvest has failed to meet this minimum purchase threshold in the following periods:

> • **Q3 2023 (July -- September 2023):** Prairie Harvest\'s purchases from Greenfield represented approximately 58% of its total Organic and Natural Food Product purchases by dollar volume, falling twelve (12) percentage points below the contractual minimum.
>
> • **Q4 2023 (October -- December 2023):** Prairie Harvest\'s purchases from Greenfield represented approximately 52% of its total Organic and Natural Food Product purchases by dollar volume, reflecting a further decline from the prior quarter.
>
> • **January 2024:** Prairie Harvest\'s purchases from Greenfield represented approximately 49% of its total Organic and Natural Food Product purchases by dollar volume, marking the lowest level of compliance during the term of the Agreement.

Greenfield\'s account management team notified Prairie Harvest of these deficiencies verbally on multiple occasions, including during a telephone call between the undersigned and you on October 12, 2023, and in a formal written notice sent on December 5, 2023. Despite these communications and the opportunities provided to correct course, Prairie Harvest\'s purchasing compliance continued to decline rather than improve. A detailed compliance report for the periods identified above is enclosed with this letter.

**Violation of Section 9.1 --- Minimum Advertised Price Policy**

Section 9.1 of the ADA provides: \"Dealer agrees not to advertise any Greenfield-branded product at a price below the Minimum Advertised Price established by Greenfield and communicated to Dealer via the Greenfield Dealer Portal.\" Greenfield has documented the following violations of this provision by Prairie Harvest:

> • **August 3, 2023:** Prairie Harvest advertised Greenfield Premium Quinoa Blend at \$8.49 per unit in its weekly print flyer and on its website. The Minimum Advertised Price for this product is \$11.49. Prairie Harvest was notified of this violation in writing on August 3, 2023.
>
> • **September 19, 2023:** Prairie Harvest advertised Greenfield Organic Harvest Trail Mix at \$5.99 per unit in an in-store promotional display and on social media. The Minimum Advertised Price for this product is \$8.29. Prairie Harvest was notified of this violation in writing on September 19, 2023.
>
> • **November 8, 2023:** Prairie Harvest advertised Greenfield Premium Quinoa Blend at \$7.99 per unit in-store and online --- a price even lower than the initial August 3 violation. The Minimum Advertised Price for this product remains \$11.49. This violation was discussed in a direct email from the undersigned to you on November 8, 2023, in which Prairie Harvest was expressly warned that continued non-compliance would jeopardize the dealer relationship.

In addition, Greenfield\'s field representatives have confirmed that Prairie Harvest is not merely advertising below MAP but is in fact transacting sales of Greenfield-branded products at these below-MAP price points in its retail locations. This pattern of below-MAP advertising and selling constitutes a repeated material breach of the Agreement and materially undermines Greenfield\'s brand positioning in the marketplace. A summary of documented MAP violations is enclosed with this letter.

**Cumulative Breach and Opportunity to Cure**

Greenfield provided Prairie Harvest with multiple opportunities to cure the breaches described above, including formal written warnings dated August 3, 2023, September 19, 2023, November 8, 2023, and December 5, 2023, as well as numerous verbal communications between the parties\' respective management teams. Rather than improving, Prairie Harvest\'s non-compliance with both Section 7.2 and Section 9.1 has worsened over time, as the data set forth above demonstrates. The cumulative and repeated nature of these violations constitutes \"repeated material breaches\" within the meaning of Section 12.4 of the Agreement. Greenfield has therefore determined, in its sole discretion as permitted by the Agreement, to exercise its right to terminate the Agreement for cause, effective April 30, 2024.

**Post-Termination Obligations**

Effective April 30, 2024, Prairie Harvest must comply with the following post-termination obligations under the Agreement:

1\. **Cessation of Branding Use.** Prairie Harvest shall immediately cease all use of the Greenfield trade name, trademarks, logos, and branding materials in all advertising, signage, promotional materials, and digital media, including but not limited to its website, social media accounts, and printed collateral.

2\. **Inventory Sell-Through.** Prairie Harvest may sell through remaining Greenfield-branded inventory on hand as of April 30, 2024, within sixty (60) days (i.e., by June 29, 2024), provided that during this sell-through period Prairie Harvest shall not advertise or sell any Greenfield-branded products at prices below the applicable Minimum Advertised Price then in effect, in accordance with Greenfield\'s standard MAP pricing. Any unsold Greenfield-branded inventory remaining after June 29, 2024 must be returned to Greenfield at Greenfield\'s expense pursuant to Section 13.2 of the Agreement.

3\. **Outstanding Balances.** Prairie Harvest shall remit all outstanding balances owed to Greenfield within thirty (30) days of the effective termination date.

**Closing**

Greenfield regrets the necessity of this action but has an obligation to protect the integrity of its authorized dealer network and the brand standards that benefit all participants in that network. We are willing to facilitate an orderly transition and encourage you to contact Greenfield\'s account management team at your earliest convenience to coordinate logistics related to inventory, branding materials, and final account reconciliation. Nothing in this letter shall be construed as a waiver of any of Greenfield\'s rights or remedies under the Agreement or at law, all of which are expressly reserved. Should you have any questions regarding this notice, please do not hesitate to contact me directly or reach out to Greenfield\'s General Counsel, Patricia Hong.

Very truly yours,

GREENFIELD ORGANICS, INC.

B(" The Complaint omits that \"Prairie Harvest disclosed in their application that Greenfield Organics terminated its dealer agreement,\" which defeats the \"insider knowledge\" inference (¶¶ 88, 152). It also omits that Heartland would be \"happy to proceed with standard onboarding\" if PH cleared review, and that the review sought routine items (updated financials, trade references, credit report). Ex. C describes a conditional credit hold, not a refusal.", "Ex. C (Marsh):")
B(" The Complaint quotes the first sentence of § 9.3 but omits the second paragraph confirming dealer pricing discretion. It omits § 9.1’s express carve-out for transaction prices, Ex. C § 5, § 12.3 (no-cause termination) and § 12.4(d) (repeated-violation termination without cure). It also mislabels § 12.2 as a termination provision.", "Ex. A (ADA):")
B(" The Complaint says the letter did not invoke § 9.3 (¶ 96) and that it gave no cure opportunity (¶ 102). The letter grounds termination in § 12.4, recounts four written and multiple verbal notices, and expressly exceeds the 30-day notice requirement.", "Termination letter:")

# ---------- IV. Claim-by-claim ----------
H("IV. Claim-by-Claim Analysis")
H("A. Counts I and V: Exclusive Dealing (Sherman § 1; Clayton § 3)", 2)
P("Exclusive dealing is judged under the rule of reason under both statutes. The plaintiff must plausibly allege a relevant market, substantial foreclosure of rivals in that market, and resulting harm to competition (higher prices, reduced output or quality), not merely harm to a dealer. Tampa Electric, 365 U.S. 320; Roland Machinery, 749 F.2d at 394 (exclusive dealing is unlawful only if it is likely to keep at least one significant competitor from doing business in the relevant market and probably will raise prices or reduce output). In the Seventh Circuit the § 1 and Clayton § 3 standards have largely converged.", "Legal standard. ")
P("", "Defects:")
N(" As shown in Part III.B, the pleaded 15.4% is overstated (correctly about 10% or less even on the plaintiff’s method) and falls below the levels courts have found meaningful. The dispositive points are the short, terminable terms (§§ 12.2–12.3) and the open 30%. The Complaint never alleges that any rival distributor was unable to reach efficient scale, that any rival exited, or that distribution prices rose. Tallgrass, NorthStar and roughly 40 others remain active, and the fringe holds 36%.", "No substantial foreclosure.")
N(" A 70% requirement with a 30% carve-out, § 7.3 exclusions, and a 90-day exit right is not de facto exclusivity of the kind condemned in ZF Meritor or Dentsply (United States v. Dentsply Int’l, Inc., 399 F.3d 181 (3d Cir. 2005)), both of which involved firms with dominant shares. Compare Concord Boat Corp. v. Brunswick Corp., 207 F.3d 1039 (8th Cir. 2000) (no foreclosure where customers could and did switch).", "Partial exclusivity by a 22% firm.")
N(" PH is a dealer, not a foreclosed rival distributor. Its alleged injury is that, after termination, it lacked alternative supply relationships (¶¶ 129, 191). That injury flows from the termination, a unilateral act that Greenfield was contractually entitled to take on 90 days’ notice in any event, and not from any reduction in competition among distributors. Brunswick Corp. v. Pueblo Bowl-O-Mat, Inc., 429 U.S. 477, 489 (1977); Atlantic Richfield Co. v. USA Petroleum Co., 495 U.S. 328 (1990). PH’s premise (that the ADA prevented alternative relationships) is also contradicted by its own continuous purchases from four rival distributors. Note that in pari delicto is not a defense to an antitrust claim (Perma Life Mufflers, Inc. v. International Parts Corp., 392 U.S. 134 (1968)), so we should not argue that PH is barred because it signed the ADA; the argument is the absence of antitrust injury.", "No antitrust injury.")
N(" The justifications are recited in § 7.2 itself (planning, upstream purchasing leverage, service levels) and backed by reciprocal benefits (Ex. B volume discounts of up to 8%, priority allocation under § 3.3, marketing support under § 6.2). These are classic efficiencies (cf. Roland Machinery). Justifications are typically a merits issue, but the face of the contract makes ¶ 60’s \"no legitimate justification\" allegation implausible.", "Procompetitive justifications on the face of the ADA.")
N(" Clayton § 3 applies only to the sale or lease of \"goods, wares, merchandise ... or other commodities.\" Plaintiff defines the relevant market as distribution services (¶¶ 32–33), and its theory of foreclosure concerns distribution services. This is a credible argument for dismissing Count V, or at least for confining it. We should expect the response that the ADA is a contract for the sale of food products, and the dominant-purpose test may cut against us, so this should be presented as an alternative ground. Count V also duplicates Count I and adds nothing; a § 3 claim that fails the § 1 rule-of-reason analysis fails generally.", "Count V: services versus goods.")
N(" PH is no longer a dealer and is not bound by § 7.2. It faces no threatened loss from enforcement of § 7.2 against other dealers and lacks standing under Clayton § 16 to enjoin Greenfield’s contracts with third parties (Prayer ¶ (d)(i)).", "Injunctive relief.")
P("High likelihood of dismissal or eventual summary judgment. If the court permits amendment, plaintiff will try to plead rival-level effects through Aldersgate; the terminability and partial-exclusivity points remain strong.", "Assessment: ")

H("B. Count II: Minimum Resale Price Maintenance (Sherman § 1)", 2)
P("Vertical minimum RPM is judged under the rule of reason. Leegin Creative Leather Products, Inc. v. PSKS, Inc., 551 U.S. 877 (2007). A manufacturer or supplier may announce a pricing policy and refuse to deal with non-compliant dealers without forming an \"agreement\" (United States v. Colgate & Co., 250 U.S. 300 (1919)). Dealer complaints followed by termination do not by themselves show a price agreement (Monsanto Co. v. Spray-Rite Service Corp., 465 U.S. 752 (1984); Business Electronics Corp. v. Sharp Electronics Corp., 485 U.S. 717 (1988)). MAP policies that restrict advertising but not transaction prices are generally analyzed as non-price restraints and are routinely upheld. Even an RPM agreement requires proof of harm to interbrand competition, which ordinarily requires market power in the relevant interbrand market.", "Legal standard. ")
P("", "Our defenses:")
N(" The Complaint does not allege that Greenfield-Branded Products (the only products subject to MAP, a subset of the 12,000+ SKUs and of PH’s purchases) have any market power in any retail product market (e.g., packaged quinoa or grains). The market it pleads is wholesale distribution services, which is the wrong market for an RPM claim. Leegin focuses on interbrand competition, and the Complaint alleges only suppressed intrabrand competition (¶¶ 108, 137). Its assertion that Greenfield has not justified the policy (¶ 141) inverts the burden.", "No interbrand market or market power pleaded.")
N(" § 9.1 expressly excludes transaction prices. Ex. C § 3 and § 5 disclaim any minimum resale price, and § 9.3 acknowledges that \"retail pricing is ultimately within Dealer’s discretion.\" The documented violations were advertising violations: print flyers, the website, social media, and online and in-store advertising.", "Contract text.")
N(" Greenfield’s stated termination ground was § 12.4 (repeated § 9.1 and § 7.2 breaches), not § 9.3. A unilateral decision to terminate a dealer that breached advertising and purchase-volume obligations is lawful under Colgate and Monsanto.", "Termination ground.")
N(" A properly structured MAP program addresses free-riding on Greenfield’s advertising, marketing and point-of-sale support (§ 6.2) and protects brand positioning, which are recognized justifications under Leegin.", "Procompetitive rationale.")
P("Our vulnerabilities on this count are real and are discussed in Part V. In brief: (i) § 9.3 on its face reaches the price at which a dealer \"sells\"; (ii) the Nov. 8 email’s \"More importantly ... actually selling it at that price point in-store\" sentence; (iii) the same email’s reference to complaints from \"two other accounts in central Illinois asking why they should bother maintaining their pricing\", which plaintiff will use to argue a dealer-driven price-maintenance understanding; (iv) the termination letter’s statement that PH was \"transacting sales ... at these below-MAP price points,\" which \"materially undermines Greenfield’s brand positioning\" (the § 9.3 standard); and (v) the termination letter’s sell-off condition that PH \"shall not advertise or sell\" Greenfield-branded products below MAP. That condition goes beyond ADA § 12.5(b), which requires only continued compliance with the MAP (advertising) policy, and it is the closest thing in the record to an express minimum resale price term. Because the ADA is itself an express agreement, plaintiff will argue that the Colgate unilateral-policy safe harbor does not apply to the pricing provisions.", "Exposure. ")
P("Moderate. We have a strong rule-of-reason argument (no interbrand market power, no plausibly alleged anticompetitive effect) and should move to dismiss Count II. Even so, a court could find the agreement element plausibly pleaded and allow amendment to plead a retail product market. Even if the claim survives, the plaintiff faces a difficult rule-of-reason case and damages limited to injury caused by the alleged RPM. That injury is hard to separate from the independent § 7.2 ground and the 90-day no-cause right.", "Assessment: ")
P("If plaintiff argues that Illinois law treats RPM more strictly than Leegin, our response is that Illinois courts construe the Act in harmony with federal precedent (740 ILCS 10/11). We should confirm there is no Illinois-specific RPM provision or post-Leegin Illinois authority to the contrary (to be verified).", "Illinois-law caution: ")

H("C. Count III: Group Boycott / Concerted Refusal to Deal (Sherman § 1)", 2)
P("A § 1 conspiracy claim requires facts plausibly suggesting an actual agreement, not merely parallel conduct consistent with independent action. Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 556–57 (2007). Parallel conduct must be accompanied by \"plus factors.\" In re Text Messaging Antitrust Litigation, 630 F.3d 622 (7th Cir. 2010). Per se treatment of boycotts is limited to horizontal agreements among competitors that typically cut off access to a supply, facility or market necessary to compete, usually where the boycotters have market power. Northwest Wholesale Stationers, Inc. v. Pacific Stationery & Printing Co., 472 U.S. 284 (1985); NYNEX Corp. v. Discon, Inc., 525 U.S. 128 (1998).", "Legal standard. ")
P("", "Defects:")
N(" Greenfield terminated PH on March 15, 2024, four weeks before the MOTA conference (April 12–14) where the agreement was supposedly formed (¶¶ 84–85, 149). Greenfield’s refusal to deal therefore cannot have been pursuant to that agreement; it was a pre-existing unilateral contract termination. Pleading it as \"a continuation\" (¶ 79) does not convert a unilateral act into a concerted one.", "The chronology defeats Greenfield’s participation.")
N(" Each conspiracy allegation (attendance, discussions, agreement) is pleaded \"on information and belief\" (¶¶ 83–84, 90) with no who, what, when or where. Attendance at a large industry conference is the kind of \"opportunity to conspire\" that is insufficient under Twombly. A cross-supply agreement for niche specialty products (¶ 41) is a legitimate collaboration and not a plus factor.", "Opportunity is not agreement.")
N(" PH itself told Heartland about the termination in its application. Heartland applied \"standard new account procedure, just with the extra layer\" because PH had just lost its largest supplier relationship, which is a facially rational credit concern. It said it was \"happy to proceed\" if PH cleared the review. The email supports independent, self-interested action and shows no refusal at all. The Complaint never alleges that Heartland made a final refusal after the review or that PH supplied the requested financials, trade references and credit report.", "Exhibit C refutes the inference plaintiff draws from it.")
N(" The only Great Lakes allegations are that it \"failed to process\" an application \"in a timely manner\" and \"ultimately declined\" (¶ 89). No date, communication or decision-maker is identified. Great Lakes was also an existing supplier whose PH volume had fallen 44% from FY2021 to FY2023.", "Great Lakes allegations are bare conclusions.")
N(" Plaintiff never explains why Heartland and Great Lakes, Greenfield’s direct competitors, would forgo a $38 million retailer’s business to enforce Greenfield’s MAP policy on Greenfield-branded products. A rival distributor gains nothing from propping up a competitor’s brand prices, and the Complaint itself pleads that each had an independent incentive to win the account (¶ 80). Plaintiff will frame this as \"action against self-interest\" (a plus factor). The answer is that Ex. C supplies the independent explanation, and there was no refusal, only a credit hold.", "No plausible motive for the alleged co-conspirators.")
N(" The alleged arrangement mixes a vertical termination (Greenfield–PH) with alleged horizontal refusals. NYNEX bars per se treatment of vertical elements. Even as to the horizontal elements, the alleged boycotters hold 48%, and the remaining 52% (Tallgrass, NorthStar, about 40 others) stayed open to PH and supplied it (¶¶ 78, 105). Under Northwest Stationers there is no denial of an essential input. Under the rule of reason, there is no pleaded harm to competition as opposed to harm to one retailer among thousands.", "Per se treatment is unavailable and rule of reason fails.")
P("Strong Twombly motion. This is nonetheless the count with the most discovery risk, because the outcome depends on what Greenfield personnel actually said to Heartland and Great Lakes. Before we argue in a brief that no communications occurred, we must confirm through the internal investigation (Part VIII) that there were none: no MOTA conversations, no emails under the cross-supply relationship, no \"heads-up\" calls about PH. Note also that a proven boycott would expose Greenfield to joint and several liability for the entire trebled amount with no right of contribution (Texas Industries, Inc. v. Radcliff Materials, Inc., 451 U.S. 630 (1981)), which is likely why plaintiff named the co-conspirators as non-parties.", "Assessment: ")

H("D. Count IV: Monopolization and Attempted Monopolization (Sherman § 2)", 2)
P("Monopolization requires monopoly power in a relevant market plus willful acquisition or maintenance of that power by exclusionary conduct. United States v. Grinnell Corp., 384 U.S. 563, 570–71 (1966). Attempted monopolization requires predatory or anticompetitive conduct, specific intent, and a dangerous probability of achieving monopoly power. Spectrum Sports, Inc. v. McQuillan, 506 U.S. 447, 456 (1993).", "Legal standard. ")
N(" Courts generally require a share above 50%, and usually much higher, before inferring monopoly power (see, e.g., Blue Cross & Blue Shield United of Wisconsin v. Marshfield Clinic, 65 F.3d 1406, 1411 (7th Cir. 1995) (50% as a minimum)). A 22% share fails as a matter of law. The rival shares (15%, 11%, 9%, 7%) and the 36% fringe confirm the absence of power to control price or exclude competition. The Complaint pleads no supracompetitive pricing or output restriction beyond conclusions (¶ 168).", "No monopoly power.")
N(" Shares below roughly 30% rarely support a dangerous probability of success. Even plaintiff’s own projection reaches only about 28.7% in five years. Barriers are undercut by the presence of about 45 distributors, the 36% fringe, and PH’s own ability to source from 20+ vendors.", "No dangerous probability.")
N(" Combining three firms (48%) to reach a monopoly-like share is an impermissible \"shared monopoly\" theory, which § 2 does not recognize. Collective conduct is a § 1 issue. The Complaint’s § 2 power allegations rest on the fabricated 3,730 HHI (¶¶ 165, 176).", "\"Shared monopoly\" is not cognizable.")
N(" Specific intent is inferred from share growth (¶ 173(a)), which is consistent with competition on the merits, and from the same conduct whose § 1 deficiencies are addressed above. Conduct that is not anticompetitive under § 1 does not become exclusionary under § 2 when relabeled.", "Specific intent and conduct.")
P("Highest-probability dismissal, potentially with prejudice, since no amendment can raise a 22% share to monopoly levels.", "Assessment: ")

H("E. Count VI: Illinois Antitrust Act (740 ILCS 10/3)", 2)
B(" The Act directs courts to construe it with reference to federal antitrust decisions (740 ILCS 10/11). Count VI repleads Counts I–III and falls with them.", "Derivative.")
B(" Count VI cites \"10/3\" generally without identifying the subsection violated (10/3(1)–(4) cover different conduct and carry different remedies). It should be dismissed or repleaded with specificity.", "No subsection pleaded.")
B(" Under 740 ILCS 10/7(2), we understand treble damages to be limited to violations of particular subsections, and actual damages to apply otherwise (to be verified). The Complaint seeks blanket treble damages (¶ 203).", "Trebling limited.")
B(" Fees are sought \"pursuant to 740 ILCS 10/5\" (¶ 203; Prayer ¶ (e)). Section 5 appears to be the Act’s exemptions provision, and fees are addressed in 10/7 (to be verified). This is a further sign of hurried drafting.", "Wrong fee provision.")
B(" To the extent any federal claim survives, the state claim survives with it. If all federal claims are dismissed, we should ask the court either to dismiss Count VI on the merits under the harmonization principle or, alternatively, to decline supplemental jurisdiction (28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3)). Choose deliberately: a remand-style dismissal sends the case to Illinois state court, where § 14.3 still requires Cook County.", "Supplemental jurisdiction.")

H("F. Count VII: Tortious Interference with Business Relations (Illinois common law)", 2)
P("Under Illinois law, the plaintiff must allege (1) a reasonable expectancy of entering into a valid business relationship; (2) the defendant’s knowledge of it; (3) intentional and unjustified interference that prevented the expectancy from ripening; and (4) damages. The interference must be directed at third parties. See, e.g., Fellhauer v. City of Geneva, 142 Ill. 2d 495 (1991).", "Legal standard. ")
N(" Theory (a) (terminating the ADA) concerns Greenfield’s own relationship with PH. A party cannot tortiously interfere with its own contract, and exercising an express contractual termination right is privileged. Any dispute about the validity of the termination sounds in contract, a claim PH has notably chosen not to plead, likely to avoid §§ 13.1–13.2 and 14.4.", "No interference with a third-party relationship.")
N(" A generalized reference to \"retail customers\" and \"producers, manufacturers, and other distributors\" (¶¶ 206–207) is insufficient. Illinois requires specific third parties and conduct directed at them.", "No identified expectancy.")
N(" Theories (b) and (c) are the boycott and exclusive-dealing theories, and the only \"improper means\" pleaded are the antitrust violations (¶ 210). They fall with Counts I–III.", "Derivative.")
N(" § 13.1 waives lost profits and consequential damages for claims \"arising out of or related to this Agreement ... whether based on contract, tort ... or any other ... theory,\" and § 13.2 caps aggregate liability at the prior 12 months’ payments (roughly $6.8 million). Plaintiff pleads \"willful, wanton, and malicious\" conduct (¶ 212) to invoke the § 13.3(d) willful-misconduct exclusion; we should hold plaintiff to that. (Contractual limitations generally cannot waive prospective federal antitrust treble-damages liability, so §§ 13.1–13.2 should be invoked only against Count VII and any contract-based theory, not against Counts I–VI.)", "Contractual limitations.")
N(" § 14.4 awards prevailing-party fees in any proceeding \"to resolve any dispute arising hereunder.\" Count VII, which is premised on the ADA termination, is a strong candidate. The antitrust counts arguably are too. This gives us leverage and an asymmetric risk for plaintiff.", "Fee-shifting.")
P("Weak; good motion-to-dismiss candidate.", "Assessment: ")

The workbook concedes the margin was \"applied directly to cost of goods purchased, not resale revenue\" and was chosen \"[p]er counsel instruction.\" PH’s actual gross margin is 31.4% (FY2023), and the workbook cites an industry range of 28–35%. # ---------- VII. Procedural ----------
H("VII. Procedural and Contractual Issues")
B(" ADA § 14.2 requires 30 days of good-faith senior-executive negotiation before \"any formal legal proceeding\" on disputes \"arising out of or relating to\" the ADA. Determine whether PH ever served a § 14.2 notice. If it did not, raise non-compliance in the motion, as a ground for a stay or as a further sign of bad faith. It is unlikely to be dispositive of statutory antitrust claims.", "Pre-suit negotiation.")

B(" The court may consider the ADA (Ex. A), the Alvarez chain (Ex. B), the Marsh email (Ex. C) and the termination letter (referenced in ¶¶ 74, 96, and central to the claims) without converting the motion. PH’s workbook generally may not be used on a 12(b)(6) motion. The Aldersgate summary (Ex. D) is incorporated, but it is plaintiff’s advocacy and should be attacked, not adopted.", "Documents properly considered on Rule 12(b)(6).")
B(" Confirm the service date and the responsive-pleading deadline (21 days after service, or 60 days if service was waived; Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(a)). Seek a stipulated extension and a schedule that defers discovery pending the motion. A motion to stay discovery pending a Twombly motion is well grounded in antitrust cases.", "Deadlines.")
B(" The four-year Clayton Act limitations period (15 U.S.C. § 15b) poses no obstacle to PH. It is relevant, however, to any claims by other dealers.", "Limitations.")

P("The Complaint (¶ 43) computes HHI as 48² + 9² + 7² + 36² = 3,730. This contains two independent errors. HHI measures the structure of independent firms; it is not evidence of coordination. Second, it treats the approximately 40 fringe distributors, which hold 36% collectively, as one firm, which inflates the index by roughly 1,264 points on its own. Correctly computed from the Complaint’s own share table, the five named firms contribute 22² + 15² + 11² + 9² + 7² = 960. Even if the 36% fringe were spread across 40 equal firms (0.9% each), they would add only about 32 points, for a total HHI of roughly 990.")
P("An HHI of about 990 is unconcentrated under both the 2010 Horizontal Merger Guidelines the Complaint cites (below 1,500) and the 2023 Merger Guidelines that superseded them (highly concentrated is above 1,800, not 2,500; the Complaint relies on a superseded threshold). HHI is in any event a merger-screening tool. Plaintiff’s own numbers therefore describe a fragmented market of about 45 distributors in which no firm holds more than 22%. That undercuts market power for every count. It also undercuts the \"oligopolistic structure\" said to facilitate coordination (¶¶ 39–44), since three firms with a combined 48% leave 52% of the market to independent rivals.")

H("F. The Complaint misquotes and selectively excerpts its own exhibits", 2)
P("Where an exhibit contradicts the pleading, the exhibit controls (Fed. R. Civ. P. 10(c); see, e.g., Bogie v. Rosenberg, 705 F.3d 603, 609 (7th Cir. 2013)). The motion should put the full texts in front of the court:")
B(" The block quote in ¶ 71 (\"Eli --- we’ve noticed your stores advertising ... We need to discuss this before it becomes a bigger issue.\") does not appear in the actual Nov. 8, 2023 email; it is a composite paraphrase. The real email leads with advertising (\"Our field representatives have confirmed that Prairie Harvest is advertising ... at $7.99 across at least three of your twelve retail locations\") and cites Section 9.1. ¶ 70 attributes the phrase \"growing concern\" to the Sept. 19 email, but that phrase does not appear in it. The Ex. B subject line also differs from the actual email. Note that the full email is not uniformly helpful (see Part V).", "Ex. B (Alvarez):")

It also omits that Heartland would be \"happy to proceed with standard onboarding\" if PH cleared review, and that the review sought routine items (updated financials, trade references, credit report). Ex. C describes a conditional credit hold, not a refusal.", "Ex. C (Marsh):")

C § 5, § 12.3 (no-cause termination) and § 12.4(d) (repeated-violation termination without cure). It also mislabels § 12.2 as a termination provision.", "Ex. A (ADA):")
